how: Lithium is the charge carrier in lithium-ion cells. Lithium carbonate or hydroxide goes into the cathode (NMC, NCA, LFP) and the electrolyte salt, and the amount sets how much energy a cell can store.
Cobalt stabilises the layered structure of NMC and NCA cathodes, which improves lifetime and safety. LFP cells use none, so demand depends on the chemistry mix.
Nickel raises the energy density of NMC and NCA cathodes, so high-nickel cells give more range per kilogram.
Stainless and alloy steels containing nickel are used in some turbine parts that must resist corrosion, especially offshore.
Nickel alloys such as Inconel are used in reactor internals and steam generators because they resist heat and corrosion.
Alkaline electrolysers use nickel electrodes and nickel-coated plates, making it a core material for large-scale green hydrogen.
Graphite is the anode material in almost every lithium-ion cell. A typical EV battery holds tens of kilograms of it.
Nuclear-grade graphite is a moderator and reflector in some reactor designs, including gas-cooled reactors.
Manganese is a cathode component in NMC, LMO and LMFP cells, where it lowers cost and reduces the need for cobalt and nickel.
Copper foil is the current collector on the anode, and copper wiring and busbars connect cells and packs.
Copper cabling, ribbons and inverter parts carry power from the panels, and some cell designs use copper instead of silver for the contacts.
A wind turbine contains tonnes of copper in generator windings, cables and transformers, and offshore farms need far more for their export cables.
Copper is the standard conductor in cables, transformers and motors. Grid expansion and electrification are the biggest drivers of new copper demand.
Copper alloys are used in condenser tubes, cabling and generators in nuclear plants.
Copper provides the electrical connections and busbars in electrolysers and fuel-cell stacks.
Neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium and terbium make the permanent magnets in most EV traction motors.
Direct-drive and some geared offshore turbines use NdFeB permanent magnets, with dysprosium and terbium added so they keep working when hot.
Rare-earth magnets appear in high-efficiency motors, generators and sensors across power systems.
Phosphate, as iron phosphate, is the cathode of LFP batteries, now the most common chemistry for lower-cost EVs and grid storage.
Silicon is blended into graphite anodes, and is being developed as a replacement, because it can hold much more lithium per gram.
High-purity polysilicon is made into the wafers used in the large majority of solar cells.
Silver paste forms the fine conducting lines on most silicon solar cells. Solar is one of silver's largest industrial uses.
Silver is used as a catalyst and contact material in some fuel cells and electrolysers, mainly alkaline types.
Aluminium foil is the cathode current collector, and many pack casings and cooling plates are aluminium.
Panel frames and mounting structures are mostly aluminium.
Aluminium is used in some nacelle housings and cable components, though far less than steel or copper.
Aluminium conductors carry most high-voltage overhead lines, and aluminium is a lower-cost alternative to copper in distribution cables.
Bauxite is the ore for the aluminium used in panel frames and mounting structures.
Bauxite is the ore for aluminium, the main metal in overhead transmission lines.
Cadmium telluride thin-film panels, the main non-silicon solar technology, use tellurium as the light-absorbing layer. It is mostly a by-product of copper refining.
Indium tin oxide is a transparent contact layer in heterojunction and thin-film cells, and CIGS cells use indium directly.
Gallium is a component of CIGS thin-film cells and of high-efficiency multi-junction cells.
Gallium nitride and gallium arsenide chips make compact, efficient power electronics such as chargers and converters.
Selenium is a component of CIGS thin-film solar cells.
Cadmium telluride panels use a cadmium compound as one of the two main semiconductor layers.
Zinc is the anode in zinc-air, zinc-ion and nickel-zinc batteries, which are mostly still at pilot scale.
Galvanising with zinc protects steel towers and foundations from corrosion.
Hot-dip galvanising protects pylons, substation structures and other steelwork.
Lead-acid batteries still supply much of the world's backup and starter-battery power and some grid storage.
Tin-based solder joins the metal ribbons to the cells in a solar module.
Tin solder is used in the electronics inside inverters and control systems.
Tungsten wire is increasingly used in the diamond-wire saws that slice silicon ingots into wafers.
Tungsten is a leading candidate for the plasma-facing surfaces in fusion reactors and is used for radiation shielding.
Molybdenum forms the back contact in CIGS thin-film cells.
Molybdenum is alloyed into steels for gearboxes, shafts and towers to give strength and fatigue resistance.
Molybdenum steels and alloys are used in power-plant and transmission equipment.
Molybdenum is an alloying element in reactor pressure-vessel and structural steels that must withstand heat and radiation.
Vanadium redox flow batteries store energy in vanadium electrolyte, which suits long-duration grid storage.
Vanadium is added to high-strength steels used in towers and structural parts.
Stainless and alloy steels need chromium, and some turbine components use them.
Chromium in stainless steels and alloys gives reactor components their corrosion resistance.
Stainless-steel plates and pipework in electrolysers depend on chromium.
Steel racking and trackers support utility-scale solar farms.
Steel makes up most of a turbine by weight, in the tower, nacelle frame and foundation.
Pylons, substation structures and transformer cores (electrical steel) are all steel.
Reactor vessels, containment structures and pipework are steel.
Titanium resists corrosion and is used in condenser tubes and some reactor components.
PEM electrolysers use titanium plates and porous transport layers because they survive the acidic, high-voltage conditions.
Titanium minerals are the ore for the titanium metal used in electrolyser components.
Zirconium alloys form the cladding around fuel pellets in most reactors because they let neutrons pass. Hafnium, a by-product, is used in control rods.
Niobium microalloying strengthens the steel used in towers and structures.
Niobium-titanium superconducting wire is used in MRI machines and in superconducting cables and magnets.
Niobium is used in some reactor alloys and in the superconducting magnets planned for fusion.
Tantalum capacitors are used in power electronics and control systems.
Platinum is the main catalyst in PEM fuel cells and is also used in PEM electrolysers.
Palladium membranes purify hydrogen, and palladium is used in some catalysts and sensors.
Antimony hardens the lead in lead-acid battery plates.
Antimony oxide helps clarify the glass used in solar panels.
Boron is the dopant in p-type silicon cells and a component of the borosilicate glass in some modules.
Boron is a constituent of the NdFeB magnets in wind turbine generators.
Boron-10 absorbs neutrons and is used in reactor control rods and shielding.
Fluorspar is the source of the fluorine in the LiPF6 electrolyte salt and in PVDF binders.
Fluoropolymers made from fluorspar are used in some module backsheets and coatings.
Fluorine is needed to make UF6, the gas used to enrich uranium for reactor fuel.
The fluorinated membranes in PEM electrolysers and fuel cells depend on fluorine chemicals.
High-purity silica sand is melted into the glass that covers solar panels.
Zinc-bromine flow batteries use a bromine-based electrolyte.
Gold plating is used on connectors and contacts in electronics and control equipment.
Gallium arsenide cells, used in space and some concentrator systems, contain arsenic.
Helium is the coolant in high-temperature gas reactors and cools superconducting magnets.
Magnesium hydride is being developed for solid-state hydrogen storage.
